==Problem==

For some positive integer <imath>k</imath>, the repeating base-<imath>k</imath> representation of the (base-ten) fraction <imath>\frac{7}{51}</imath> is <imath>0.\overline{23}_k = 0.232323..._k</imath>. What is <imath>k</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 13 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 14 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 15 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 16 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 17</imath>

==Solution 1==

We can expand the fraction <imath>0.\overline{23}_k</imath> as follows: <imath>0.\overline{23}_k = 2\cdot k^{-1} + 3 \cdot k^{-2} + 2 \cdot k^{-3} + 3 \cdot k^{-4} + \cdots</imath>

Notice that this is equivalent to 
<cmath>2( k^{-1} + k^{-3} + k^{-5} + ... ) + 3 (k^{-2} + k^{-4} + k^{-6} + \cdots )</cmath>

By summing the geometric series and simplifying, we have <imath>\frac{2k+3}{k^2-1} = \frac{7}{51}</imath>. Solving this quadratic equation (or simply testing the answer choices) yields the answer <imath>k = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 2==

Let <imath>a = 0.2323\dots_k</imath>. Therefore, <imath>k^2a=23.2323\dots_k</imath>.

From this, we see that <imath>k^2a-a=23_k</imath>, so <imath>a = \frac{23_k}{k^2-1} = \frac{2k+3}{k^2-1} = \frac{7}{51}</imath>.

Now, similar to in Solution 1, we can either test if <imath>2k+3</imath> is a multiple of <imath>7</imath> with the answer choices, or actually solve the quadratic, so that the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
Just as in Solution 1, we arrive at the equation <imath>\frac{2k+3}{k^2-1}=\frac{7}{51}</imath>.

Therefore now, we can rewrite this as <imath>\frac{2k+3}{(k-1)(k+1)}=\frac{7}{51}=\frac{7}{3\cdot 17}</imath>. Notice that <imath>2k+3=2(k+1)+1=2(k-1)+5</imath>. As <imath>17</imath> is a prime number, we therefore must have that one of <imath>k-1</imath> and <imath>k+1</imath> is divisible by <imath>17</imath>. Now, checking each of the answer choices, this will lead us to the answer <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 4==
Assuming you are familiar with the rules for basic repeating decimals, <imath>0.232323... = \frac{23}{99}</imath>. Now we want our base, <imath>k</imath>, to conform to <imath>23\equiv7\pmod k</imath> and <imath>99\equiv51\pmod k</imath>, the reason being that we wish to convert the number from base <imath>10</imath> to base <imath>k</imath>. Given the first equation, we know that <imath>k</imath> must equal 9, 16, 23, or generally, <imath>7n+2</imath>. The only number in this set that is one of the multiple choices is <imath>16</imath>. When we test this on the second equation, <imath>99\equiv51\pmod k</imath>, it comes to be true. Therefore, our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 5==

Note that the LHS equals <cmath>\bigg(\frac{2}{k} + \frac{2}{k^3} + \cdots \bigg) + \bigg(\frac{3}{k^2} + \frac{3}{k^4} + \cdots \bigg) = \frac{\frac{2}{k}}{1 - \frac{1}{k^2}} + \frac{\frac{3}{k^2}}{1 - \frac{1}{k^2}} = \frac{2k+3}{k^2-1},</cmath> from which we see our equation becomes <cmath>\frac{2k+3}{k^2-1} = \frac{7}{51}, \ \ \implies \ \ 51(2k+3) = 7(k^2-1).</cmath> 

Note that <imath>17</imath> therefore divides <imath>k^2 - 1,</imath> but as <imath>17</imath> is prime this therefore implies <cmath>k \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{17}.</cmath> (Warning: This would not be necessarily true if <imath>17</imath> were composite.) Note that <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)} 16 }</imath> is the only answer choice congruent satisfying this modular congruence, thus completing the problem. <imath>\square</imath>

~ Professor-Mom

==Solution 6(Cheese and answer choices)==

We can find that we just estimate the first two digits and can get <imath>\frac{2}{k} + \frac{2}{k^2} = \frac{7}{51}</imath> and plug in some values and expand into <imath>\frac{2k+2}{k^2} = \frac{7}{51}</imath> and plugin some values and find that for 16, <imath>\frac{34}{256}</imath> is very close to our target of <imath>\frac{7}{51}</imath> so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 7 (Risky)==

The fraction \( 23/99 = 0.23232323... \)

We have the base representation of \( 7/51 \).

There exists some fraction \( a/b \) such that \( 7/51 \cdot a/b = 23/99 \).

\( a = 23/7 \), \( b = 99/51 \). Our fraction is then \( a/b = (23/7) / (99/51) \Rightarrow (23 \times 51) / (7 \times 99) \Rightarrow 1173/693 \).

Bases must be a multiple of the square of a number. We see that \( \sqrt{1173} \) is about 34 and \( \sqrt{693} \) is about 26. We subtract to get a common square, which is \( 34-26 = 8 \).

Our answer must be a multiple of 8, and the only one is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 8 (Also Risky)==

Notice how \( 23/99 = 0.232323232323\ldots \), but round it down to \( 0.23 \).
\( 7/51 \) is around \( 0.13 \).
We then have \( 0.23 - 0.13 = 0.1 \).

Multiply by 1000 to get \( 0.1 \times 1000 = 100 \).

The fraction is the base \( k \) number multiplied by another number divided by 100. The number that gets closest to the number 100 when multiplied by another number is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 9 (No Modular Arithmetic, Solving the Quadratic)==
<imath>0.\overline{23}_k=\dfrac{23_k}{k^2-1}=\dfrac{2\times k^1+3\times k^0}{k^2-1}=\dfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}</imath>, so our equation is just <imath>\dfrac7{51}=\dfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}</imath>, so now let's solve!

<cmath>\begin{align*}
    \dfrac7{51}&=\dfrac{2k+3}{k^2-1}\\
    7k^2-7&=102k+153\\
    7k^2-102k-160&=0,\\
\end{align*}</cmath>

and now let's solve this equation with the Quadratic Formula!

<cmath>\begin{align*}
    k&=\dfrac{-(-102)\pm\sqrt{(-102)^2-4(7)(-160)}}{2\times7}\\
    k&=\dfrac{102\pm\sqrt{10404+4480}}{14}\\
    k&=\dfrac{102\pm\sqrt{14884}}{14}\\
    k&=\dfrac{102\pm122}{14},
\end{align*}</cmath>

and we are given that <imath>k</imath> is a positive integer, so we will take the plus and not the minus since the minus will produce a negative non-integer value for <imath>k</imath> in this case. Therefore, <cmath>k=\dfrac{102+122}{14}=\dfrac{224}{14}=\boxed{16}.</cmath>

~Yuhao2012
